questions.prompt: A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m. (a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2) (b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2) (c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.10/4.80\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. (c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 3.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 18 N. A resistive force of 5 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=18-5=13$ N. $a=F/m=4.33$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.33\times4=17.33$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 3.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 18 N. A resistive force of 5 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=18-5=13$ N. $a=F/m=4.33$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.33\times4=17.33$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: Two resistors, 100 $\Omega$ and 200 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 6 V supply. (a) Calculate the current. questions.prompt: Two resistors, 220 $\Omega$ and 470 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 12 V supply. (a) Calculate the current. (2) (b) Calculate the potential difference across the 470 $\Omega$ resistor. (2) (c) Explain how the total current would change if the resistors were connected in parallel instead. (2)
questions.solution: (a) $R_T=690\,\Omega$, so $I=V/R=0.0174$ A. (b) $V_2=IR_2=8.17$ V. (c) Parallel connection gives a smaller total resistance than either branch, so for the same supply voltage the total current is larger. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: Two resistors, 220 $\Omega$ and 470 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 12 V supply. (a) Calculate the current. (2) (b) Calculate the potential difference across the 470 $\Omega$ resistor. (2) (c) Explain how the total current would change if the resistors were connected in parallel instead. (2)
questions.solution: (a) $R_T=690\,\Omega$, so $I=V/R=0.0174$ A. (b) $V_2=IR_2=8.17$ V. (c) Parallel connection gives a smaller total resistance than either branch, so for the same supply voltage the total current is larger. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: Electromagnetic radiation has frequency $5e+14$ Hz. (a) Calculate its wavelength in vacuum. (2) (b) Calculate the energy of one photon using $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s. (2) (c) Explain what is meant by diffraction and state when it is most noticeable. (3)
questions.solution: (a) $\lambda=c/f=6.000e-07$ m. (b) $E=hf=3.315e-19$ J. (c) Diffraction is spreading of waves at an aperture/edge and is greatest when the aperture size is comparable with the wavelength. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.solution: (a) $\lambda=c/f=6.667e-07$ m. (b) $E=hf=2.983e-19$ J. (c) Diffraction is spreading of waves at an aperture/edge and is greatest when the aperture size is comparable with the wavelength. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 4.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 25 N. A resistive force of 7 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=25-7=18$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 4.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 25 N. A resistive force of 7 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=25-7=18$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 4.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 25 N. A resistive force of 7 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=25-7=18$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

(2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A spherical body has mass $5.97e+24$ kg and radius $6.37e+06$ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$. (3) (b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2) (c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A spherical body has mass $7.35e+22$ kg and radius $1.74e+06$ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$. (3) (b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2) (c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=1.62$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A spherical body has mass $1.9e+27$ kg and radius $7.15e+07$ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$. (3) (b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2) (c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=24.8$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

(2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m. (a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2) (b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2) (c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. (c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]
